name: Buyout Modelling
title: Buyout Modelling
answer: Buyout modelling is the practice of building a financial model for the acquisition of a whole company, usually by a private equity fund, and testing whether the deal can return the fund's target rate over a holding period. It covers the sources and uses of funds, the debt package, projected cash flows, and the exit. In this atlas it sits inside private equity and deal sourcing, next to the wider record of merger and acquisition filings the site tracks.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Buyout modelling is the practice of building a financial model for the acquisition of a whole company, usually by a private equity fund, and testing whether the deal can return the fund's target rate over a holding period. It covers the sources and uses of funds, the debt package, projected cash flows, and the exit. In this atlas it sits inside private equity and deal sourcing, next to the wider record of merger and acquisition filings the site tracks.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a spreadsheet, most often Excel, with data pulled from company accounts, market prices, and deal documents. Larger funds add dedicated platforms for portfolio monitoring and data rooms, and increasingly a language model sits on top to draft memos or summarise filings. The site's own record of 401 merger and acquisition filings and 514 company pages is the kind of reference material a modeller checks against.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A buyout model starts with historical financials, then projects revenue, margins, and capital expenditure across the hold. The debt schedule drives interest and repayment, and the returns are solved at exit under a base, upside, and downside case. Sensitivity tables show which assumptions, usually entry multiple, leverage, and exit multiple, move the internal rate of return most.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The model is only as good as its inputs, so provenance matters: audited accounts, signed term sheets, and dated market data, with every hard coded number traceable to a source. Funds keep version control and an audit trail because the investment committee and later the limited partners will ask where a figure came from. Confidential deal information stays inside the data room and is not fed into public tools without clearance.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: More of the mechanical work, spreading accounts, building the first draft of the model, and writing the memo, is moving to software, which shifts the analyst's time toward judgement about the assumptions. Funds are also testing whether models can flag deals earlier from filings and market data. The constraint is not compute but trust: a buyout decision still needs a human who can defend every number.
